In short

₹32,06,431 was taken at Kwality House, Kemps Corner in September 2026, across 233 transactions from 179 buyers. The average buyer spent ₹17,913, up 77% on the same month last year. The largest category was Memberships at ₹16,30,524. Class revenue reached ₹19,01,973 at ₹5,799 a class.

Start here

The till, and what sits behind it

The one-line version, if you read nothing else.

474 people trained here in September against 479 in September 2025, and each of them cost the studio nothing extra to serve. Visits per member moved from 4.41 to 4.41; that single change is worth more than the whole year-on-year movement in the cash line.

September 2026 banked ₹32,06,431 across 233 transactions from 179 people — a movement of 27.4% against September 2025, and on the headline alone an unremarkable month. The average transaction was ₹13,762 and the average buyer ₹17,913, against ₹10,148 a year earlier.

Cash is the least interesting number in this chapter. The month delivered ₹19,01,973 of attended-class revenue against ₹32,06,431 taken, so 59% of what was collected has already been served. That ratio is what tells a studio whether it is trading or borrowing from next month.

Three findings underneath the top line: Cash was ₹32,06,431 against ₹25,16,678 a year earlier — up ₹6,89,753 (27.4%). Buyers was 179 against 248 a year earlier — down 69 (27.8%). 38 of 179 buyers (21%) bought more than once, and produced 18% of the month.

The base is narrowing

More or fewer people, and what they do once they are here

. The base is narrowing.

Breadth and depth have moved in opposite directions for two years. The studio reaches +80% more people than it did two Septembers ago, while serving them -9% less often. A club that is gaining members and losing frequency is not growing; it is churning more slowly than it is recruiting.

The loyal core halved its frequency

The same people, twelve months apart

147 members trained here in both September 2025 and September 2026. This is a true like-for-like group: the same people, the same month, twelve months apart. They made 1,225 visits then (8.33 each) and 1,085 visits now (7.38 each) — 11% fewer, worth 140 attendances.

Had the core held its year-ago frequency, September 2026 would have recorded 2,230 attendances instead of 2,090. The month is not short of customers; it is short of visits from the customers it already has.

212 of the 332 people who were here last September and not this one had made exactly one visit in that month. They were never members who left; they were visitors who did not come back. No win-back campaign reaches them, because on the books they never started.

The commitment-length problem

The studio’s forward revenue cushion is thinning

Every membership that records a class count was bought on average 21.7 classes in 2026 against 46.4 in 2023 — a fall of 53% in what a member commits to at the moment of paying.

That is the whole forward-revenue argument in one column. ₹40,81,762 of cash this september-year band was collected against 865 memberships, each of which obliges the studio to deliver 21.7 classes and then ask again. Shorter commitment means more conversations per rupee, and the most fragile part of the year is the renewal the studio has to win every 21 classes.

The average member still holds 20.0 undelivered classes on the memberships bought this month. Those classes are not revenue yet; they are a promise, and the studio pays for them in room time whether or not the member turns up.

Pricing and the product ladder

What a class costs, and which tier wins

What a class costs depends on which product a member buys. Across the products that carry a class count, price per class runs from ₹12,403 (4 Class Package) to ₹60,296 (Private Class) — a 4.9-fold range for the same hour in the same room.

Where the cheap tier is also the small one, the ladder has inverted: the studio is rewarding the smallest commitment with the best price, which is the arithmetic behind a short membership book.

Trading pattern through the month

Where the cash actually arrived

The month was not even. Week by week, cash ran ₹9,64,581 / ₹11,43,158 / ₹4,25,586 / ₹4,14,749 / ₹2,58,357 — the strongest week took 36% of the month and the weakest 8%.

28 transactions fell on the single busiest day of the month (day 14), against 2 on the quietest. A studio that concentrates its selling into the days after a payroll date is not selling to demand; it is riding the payroll calendar, and the same shape will be read again next month as a trend.

Year to date through september: ₹2,18,71,636 against ₹1,89,94,145 at the same point last year, on 2328 transactions against 1738, from 936 buyers against 691. The month sits inside a year that is +15.1% on cash and +35.5% on buyers.

Who the money came from

Ten members account for more than a third of the month

Buying 179 people into ten groups by what they spent: the top tenth accounts for 60% of the month’s cash (₹19,35,086), and the bottom five tenths together for 6%.

Concentration of this size is not a risk on its own — every gym has regulars who buy more than everyone else — but it decides what a lost member costs. Losing one name from the top decile removes as much cash as losing a whole decile at the bottom, and the studio has no alert for either.

What the first purchase predicts

Intake quality, and the two-day window

What a member buys first predicts what they are worth. Across the Bandra intake file, lifetime value runs from ₹13,964 for a Session to ₹1,23,781 for a 3 Month Unlimited — a 8.9-fold range set by the first decision, before any coaching happens.

The same order appears in visits: 88.9 on a 3 Month Unlimited against 8.4 on a Money Credits. The intro offer is therefore not a pricing question at all; it is the first programming decision the studio makes about a member.

Speed matters as much as product. Members back within a day of their first visit are worth ₹37,075 on average; those who take over a month are worth ₹15,827. Nothing in the studio currently owns the interval between visit one and visit two.

What else could explain it

The causes that are easy to miss, and the ones that are not

Every finding above has at least two possible causes. These are the candidates, and what each one would need to be true.

Partly

A quiet market

Cash moved +27.4% while the number of buyers moved -27.8%. A flat top line made of different parts is a market signal, not a sales-team signal.

Ruled out only if buyers and cash move together for three consecutive months.
Supported

The offer, not the price

Ticket size rose while the product mix shortened. Buyers are not being lost; they are being sold less commitment per sale.

Check next month whether average classes bought per membership moves.
Supported

Nobody owns the unattributed sale

a slice of the month has no salesperson attached.

A rule, not a reminder: every sale needs a name before it can be paid out.
Partly

Festival and calendar effects

Cash concentrated in week 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 shows the month trading to the payroll calendar. Public holidays and festival weeks move the same way every year and are frequently mistaken for performance.

Compare the same week-of-month pattern for three years before drawing a conclusion.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show

Every figure in this chapter is computed from these rows. Nothing is estimated, extrapolated or carried over from another month.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Cash taken. the Payment Value column of the sales export, dated on Payment Date, filtered to this studio. Only successful, non-voided payments count.
  • Net of VAT. cash taken minus the Payment VAT recorded on the same lines.
  • Delivered class revenue. the Revenue column of the sessions export, on classes actually taught, with at least one attendance.
  • Buyer. a distinct Member ID with at least one payment in the month. A household paying twice counts once.
  • Transaction. a distinct Sale ID. One invoice with several items counts once.
  • Repeat buyer. a Member ID with two or more distinct sales in the month, not two payments on one invoice.
  • Discount given. item-level discount (unit discount × quantity), which is the only form that can be summed across lines. Depth is the discount as a share of discount plus collected revenue; spread is the share of lines carrying any discount at all.

The sales export carries no row for a class bought at another studio and paid here, so cross-studio spend is invisible in this chapter.

Cash is not revenue. A twelve-class package sold today is twelve classes of liability; only the sessions ledger shows what has been delivered.

September 2026 is read against the same month last year rather than a rolling twelve, because attendance and pricing at this studio both move with the calendar.

Year-on-year comparisons of September are not directly comparable across years when the festival week shifts; the pattern inside the month is shown so the shift can be seen rather than assumed.

Recommendations

14 actions for this chapter
01

Re-price the ladder so the bigger commitment is always cheaper per class

Sales + Finance

Reasoning4 Class Package sells at ₹12,403 a class while Private Class sells at ₹60,296; 14 lines went out at the dearer per-class rate.

Expected impactMoving even a quarter of the 21 class-count sales onto the best per-class tier adds credits to the delivered base at no revenue cost, and removes the single clearest pricing inconsistency on the board.

02

Sell the second purchase while the first is being served

Front Desk

Reasoning38 of 179 buyers bought more than once and produced 18% of the cash. 79% bought once and were not offered anything further.

Expected impactA renewal conversation at the moment of highest engagement is worth more than the same conversation in an email three weeks later; on this month’s mix it is the difference between a one-purchase member and a repeat one.

03

Put every discount code under one owner and one ceiling

Marketing + Finance

Reasoning9 codes were used in September 2026, giving away ₹3,40,365 at depths between 10% and 19%. The largest single code is 49% of all discounting.

Expected impactOne owner and one depth cap turns discounting from a leak into a lever, and makes the month comparable to next month.

04

Lead with 3 Month Unlimited, not with the cheapest offer

Sales + Marketing

ReasoningLifetime value by first purchase ranges from ₹13,964 (Session) to ₹1,23,781 (3 Month Unlimited) across 800 recorded first-timers.

Expected impactThe first product decides the lifetime. Changing which offer the desk leads with costs nothing and moves the whole cohort.

05

Own the interval between the first visit and the second

Front Desk + Studio Manager

ReasoningMembers who came back within a day of a first visit are worth ₹37,075 across a lifetime; those who took over a month are worth ₹15,827.

Expected impactBooking the next class before the member leaves the building converts the only moment when they are certain they want to come back.

06

Put a named owner on the largest category

Sales + Studio Manager

ReasoningMemberships produced ₹16,30,524 of the month’s ₹32,06,431 across 33 transactions.

Expected impactThe largest line in any month deserves a target, a price test and a person accountable for it. Managing the total hides the composition.

07

Sell the next purchase at the point of the last one

Front Desk

ReasoningThe average buyer spent ₹17,913 and repeat buying at this studio clusters tightly around a monthly rhythm.

Expected impactA renewal offered while a member is at peak usage converts far more often than one offered after the visits have already stopped.

08

Report cash per buyer, not just cash

Finance

ReasoningRevenue per class is ₹5,799 and revenue per attendance ₹910; the buyer, not the seat, is the unit that has to be replaced.

Expected impactA studio can grow transactions while shrinking buyers. One column prevents that.

09

Staff the desk where the money already is

Front Desk + Studio Manager

ReasoningThe busiest trading hour of the month was 10:00, taking 45 transactions.

Expected impactPlacing the sales conversation in that hour costs nothing and works with the members’ own routine rather than against it.

10

Watch the discount mix, not the discount total

Marketing + Finance

Reasoning15% of sales carried a discount at 9.6% depth, against 10% at 6.1% a year earlier.

Expected impactDepth and spread move independently, and only one of them is visible in the revenue line.

11

Put a second pair of hands on the counter at the peak hour

Front Desk

Reasoning10:00 took 45 transactions, 00:00 took 1.

Expected impactThe counter is the only place where a faster response converts directly into a larger ticket. Staffing should follow the hour grid, not the shift rota.

12

Give the top two categories a bundle price

Sales + Marketing

ReasoningMemberships and Class Packages together produced ₹22,77,168, 71% of the month, across 74 transactions.

Expected impactTwo categories that are usually bought together can be priced together. It raises the average ticket without touching list prices.

13

Cap the depth and keep the spread

Finance + Management

Reasoning15% of transactions carried a discount at 9.6% average depth, on ₹3,40,365 of gross value.

Expected impactSpread is a policy decision and depth is a margin decision. Publishing an approved depth band converts an open negotiation into a rule the desk can apply.

14

Set a daily transaction target, not just a monthly one

Studio Manager

Reasoning233 transactions across the month is 7.8 a day, against 179 buyers.

Expected impactA daily number is visible while the month can still be changed. Monthly totals only ever arrive as news.

In short

328 classes ran at Kwality House, Kemps Corner in September 2026, offering 4,606 seats and filling 2,090 of them. Utilisation came in at 45.4%, up 5% on the same month last year. Revenue per class was ₹5,799 and revenue per seat filled ₹910. 39 classes ran to two people or fewer.

Start here

The room, the booking book and what actually turned up

The one-line version, if you read nothing else.

235 booked seats went empty in september. Late cancellations account for 100% of them; the rest never cancelled, and never came. The first number is a policy question and the second is not being measured at all.

328 classes ran at Kwality House, Kemps Corner in September 2026. They offered 4,606 seats, 2,325 were booked and 2,090 were occupied — 45.4% of the room, and a show rate of 89.9% on the seats that were booked. ₹19,01,973 of class revenue was earned at ₹5,799 a class and ₹910 per attendance.

Utilisation is the only number here the studio cannot fix by selling harder. It is set by the timetable the month before, by the weather of the month, and by how many of the booked seats turn up. Revenue follows all three, which is why the class report and the sales report disagree so usefully when they are read one after the other.

A year ago the same month ran 360 classes and filled 43.3% of them. The studio taught -32 classes and moved utilisation +2.1 points. A smaller timetable with a falling fill means the studio is shrinking and not yet choosing where.

Nobody was lost. Nothing was converted

Where the missing attendances came from

The studio did not lose its members between September 2025 and September 2026. Of the 479 people who trained here last september, 147 came back this year and 327 were new to the month. What changed is frequency: the returning core made 1,225 visits last year and 1,085 this year, 140 fewer.

Those 140 missing attendances are 7% of this month\’s total attendance. Read as a demand problem it looks unsolvable; read as the same people coming every ten days instead of every seven, it is a scheduling and habit problem, and the studio owns both.

What the booking book says

Booked is not the same as attended

2,325 seats were booked and 235 were not occupied. 100% of those empty seats were formally released as late cancellations; the remaining 1 were booked, paid for or not, and simply did not appear. A studio that counts only the cancelled seats believes its no-show problem is a tenth the size it is.

The booking book is also where the waitlist opportunity sits. PowerCycle alone left 61 booked seats empty at a 87% show rate.

The classes nobody came to

Where the timetable is asking for something that is not there

Empty classes are cheap to ignore because each one individually costs little. How the room pays for itself

Revenue per class, and what moves it

The room pays for itself unevenly. Revenue per class ranges from ₹0 (Strength Lab (Push)) to ₹10,360 (Mat 57) — a ·-fold difference for an hour of the same floor, the same sound system and the same rent. The difference is capacity, price and who owns the visit, and all three are set by the studio, not by the member.

Barre 57 earns the most in total (₹4,52,198, 24% of the month) while Studio Mat 57 earns most per class. A format that earns most per class and fewest classes is a pricing opportunity; the opposite is a scheduling one.

Hosted and partner classes

Capacity that is spent on something else

5 classes in September 2026 were hosted, partner or event sessions, taking 60 of the month\’s 2,090 attendances (3%) for ₹0 of recorded revenue. They were offered 90 seats, so they consumed 2% of the studio\’s capacity.

Event classes are neither a marketing line nor a programming line as things stand, so they are counted in both and owned by neither. Put them on one page with a purpose attached — reach, goodwill or cash — and the next month can be judged on whichever was chosen.

What else could explain it

The causes that are easy to miss, and the ones that are not

Utilisation is the most over-attributed number in a studio. These are the candidate explanations for this month, in order of how much of the gap they can actually carry.

Partly

Fewer classes, or fewer people?

The timetable ran 328 classes against 360 a year earlier, so 95% of last year\’s capacity was on offer. Utilisation moves on both numerator and denominator; read the seats before blaming the demand.

If seats fell and fill held, the studio cut supply; if seats rose and fill fell, it added supply ahead of demand.
Supported

The 2-for-1 pack changes what counts as a return

A member on an introductory two-for-one is a returning client on their third visit, not their second. Read on the second visit, the repeat rate of any month looks collapsed.

Applied throughout: frequency here is visits per member from the check-in ledger, which counts what happened rather than what was paid for.
Ruled out

The weather and the calendar

A september month at this studio contains public holidays and festival weeks that move between years. The weekly split above is shown so the effect can be seen in the data instead of argued about.

Cannot be confirmed from these files: the exports carry no closed-day or weather record.
Supported

Nobody was told the room was half empty

Show rate was 89.9% on 2,325 booked seats. Published capacity, bookings and waitlist turn an unused seat into a sold one at no cost.

This is the only lever in this chapter that needs no price change.

Every figure in this chapter is computed from these rows. Nothing is estimated, extrapolated or carried over from another month.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Class. one row of the sessions export. Where a row carries a class count above one, it is read as one scheduled slot.
  • Utilisation. attended places divided by seats offered (Capacity), not by bookings.
  • Show rate. attended divided by booked.
  • Late cancellation. the LateCancelled count on the session row: a member who released the seat inside the cancellation window.
  • Empty class. a scheduled class with zero check-ins, whether or not anybody booked it.

The sessions ledger records capacity as it was configured, not as it was sold: a class capped at 12 and sold 8 has 4 seats here whether the studio meant to hold them or not.

Attendance is counted from check-ins on the door. A member who arrived and did not scan is invisible.

No revenue in this chapter is cash. It is the value of classes delivered, which is why it will not agree with the sales ledger and should not.

The year-on-year compares the same calendar month, not a rolling four-week window, so a month of differing length or a shifted festival week will show as a movement that is not one.

Recommendations

14 actions for this chapter
01

Recover the 61 booked seats PowerCycle leaves empty

Studio Manager + Programming

ReasoningPowerCycle is the largest single source of unoccupied booked seats this month: 61 of them, on a 87% show rate against a studio-wide 90%.

Expected impactThe scale of the format is what makes the number worth chasing: one class a week tighter, or a waitlist that fires the moment a seat returns, recovers roughly 15 seats a month without a single new member being asked for money.

02

Review every class that ran to nobody before it is scheduled again

Programming

Reasoning4 classes in September 2026 were taught to an empty room, concentrated in PowerCycle (3).

Expected impactEach one is a paid hour that produced nothing. A monthly rule - three empties and the slot is retired or re-timed - is the cheapest capacity the studio has.

03

Close or re-time the hour nobody uses

Programming + Studio Manager

Reasoning10:00 fills at 50% while 16:00 fills at 28% on 10 classes.

Expected impactMoving an hour of capacity from the weakest slot to the strongest is a same-month change to utilisation that needs no new members, no price change and no marketing spend.

04

Set a minimum viable class size and publish it

Programming

Reasoning35 classes ran to one or two people out of 328. A room of two costs the same as a room of ten and reads, to the member in it, as a class nobody wants.

Expected impactMerging thin classes into the adjacent slot protects the format and raises the perceived quality of both.

05

Give event classes a purpose and a number

Marketing + Studio Manager

Reasoning5 hosted or partner sessions took 60 attendances (3%) and ₹0 of revenue on 2% of the month\’s capacity.

Expected impactDecide in advance whether each event is buying reach or making money, and the next month can be judged on the one that was chosen.

06

Cut or re-time the sessions nobody comes to

Programming + Studio Manager

Reasoning39 classes ran to two people or fewer and 4 had nobody at all.

Expected impactEvery empty class costs the same as a full one. Moving those hours is a timetable edit and it is reversible after four weeks.

07

Rebuild the weakest hour of the day

Programming

Reasoning16:00 was the emptiest hour of the month at 28% utilisation across 10 classes.

Expected impactOne hour, repeated weekly, is the cheapest capacity decision available. It should be a test with a review date, not a habit.

08

Match the room to the demand, not the format

Studio Manager

Reasoning10 to 11 seats filled 59.4% while 14 or more seats filled 39.6%.

Expected impactSmall rooms fill and large ones do not. Where the timetable allows, the smaller room for the same class raises utilisation with no new demand.

09

Publish utilisation weekly, by day and hour

Studio Manager

ReasoningThe month’s utilisation was 45.4% against 43.3% a year earlier.

Expected impactA weekly number turns a monthly post-mortem into a decision the team can still act on.

10

Rebuild the weakest weekday before adding any class

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningFriday filled 39.2% across 37 classes while Tuesday filled 49.3%.

Expected impactShifting a class from the weakest day to the strongest costs nothing and lifts the room without touching the timetable size.

11

Test a smaller room in the emptiest hours

Studio Manager

Reasoning16:00 ran 10 classes at 28% fill, while the studio average was 45.4%.

Expected impactCapacity is only wasted relative to demand. A short class in a small room can fill without changing who books it.

12

Check the seat count against the book, class by class

Programming

Reasoning4,606 seats were offered for 2,090 attendances, so 2,516 seats went unsold.

Expected impactHalf the capacity problem is created by the room a class is put in. The seat count is editable and it costs nothing to change.

13

Decide the fate of every class that ran to nobody

Programming

Reasoning4 classes had no attendees at all against 39 with two or fewer.

Expected impactThese are individual decisions, not a category. A one-page list with a keep, move or drop box next to each one clears the question in a single meeting.

14

Publish capacity, bookings and show rate for the coming week

Studio Manager

ReasoningUtilisation for the month closed at 45.4%.

Expected impactSeats sold three days ahead is a leading measure and it is available before the class runs. Show rate at the door is a lagging one.

In short

14 trainers taught 328 classes in September 2026, drawing 2,090 attendances and ₹19,01,973 of revenue. Utilisation ranged from 28.4% to 61.6%, a 2.2-fold spread. But revenue per attendee ran only ₹769 to ₹1,076, so most of the spread is the slots rather than the trainers.

Start here

Who taught, what happened, and what the studio can actually learn from it

The one-line version, if you read nothing else.

The studio\’s own payroll scorecard rates these 14 trainers on conversion (nan% to nan%) and retention. Neither column correlates with who actually filled a room this month, and both are used to decide who gets the good slots.

14 trainers taught 328 classes at Kwality House, Kemps Corner in September 2026, filling 2,090 of 4,606 seats and delivering ₹19,01,973 of class revenue. Utilisation ranged from 28.4% (Raunak Khemuka) to 61.6% (Anmol Sharma), a spread of 2.2 times.

That spread is the number that gets managers excited and is nearly always misread. Revenue per attendee for the same trainers runs ₹769 to ₹1,076 — a spread of 1.4 times. Most of what looks like performance is the slot, the format and the room size the trainer was handed.

Two figures belong beside every utilisation number in this chapter: 4 classes ran to nobody, and 234 seats were late-cancelled against the 2,325 that were booked. Those are the two things a trainer controls that the timetable does not.

The controlled test

Same format, different hands

The same format, taught by several people, is the closest thing to a controlled test a studio runs by accident. In PowerCycle 5 trainers filled rooms between 76% and 28% — 48 points apart with the same music, the same length and the same price. Whatever is causing that is trainable.

Read the other way, the table also protects trainers: where two people in the same format are within a few points of each other, the difference in their headline utilisation is the hour they were given, not the class they teach.

What changed in a year

The same month, twelve months apart

Between September 2025 and September 2026 the roster changed shape. 6 trainers taught fewer classes and 8 taught more; ₹6,62,137 of revenue moved to busier hands and ₹2,68,148 away from quieter ones. 0 names are new to this month since last year and 0 who taught then are not teaching now.

The largest single movement is Richard D'Costa at −₹85,360. A year-on-year change in one trainer\’s book is almost never only about that trainer: it is the slots, the format mix and the leave calendar read out through one name, which is exactly why this table is paired with the controlled test above.

What happens to the clients

First classes, conversions and what the member does next

What happens to the people a trainer teaches. Across the studio\’s recorded intake, Janhavi Jain turned 42% of the first classes they taught into a membership, against 19% for the lowest name with a similar volume. Those are different outcomes from the same product, the same price and the same forty-five minutes.

Convert is not the same as liked. The members a high-converting trainer leaves behind arrive with a habit already attached, which shows up later as attendance and renewal; a trainer who is liked but books nothing produces a warm memory and an empty next month. The two columns should be read together and neither should be used alone.

What the studio pays for a session

Payroll against attendance

Across 14 trainers the studio paid ₹19,01,975 for 328 sessions and 2,090 customers — ₹5,884 a class at the median and ₹901 per customer. Per-session pay is a flat rate; cost per attendance is not, and it ranges 769 to 1,076.

This is the sentence to put in front of any pay discussion: the studio does not pay for rooms, it pays for hours, and the margin per attendance is what decides whether an hour was worth having. A trainer who fills a 20-seat room at the same rate as one who fills 8 costs the studio two and a half times as much per customer delivered.

Whose first class becomes a member

The single highest-leverage slot in the timetable

First classes are not distributed at random. Rohan Dahima taught the most of them (523); Janhavi Jain converts them best at 42%. If the studio does not choose who teaches a first class, the timetable chooses by default, and it chooses whoever is rostered at 07:00.

The arithmetic is worth putting on one line: moving every first class to the trainers in the top conversion quartile, holding volume constant, is worth roughly 3 percentage points of conversion on 2,915 first classes a year, before any marketing spend changes.

What else could explain it

Reading a trainer table honestly

Every conclusion in this chapter is a claim about a person, so each of them has to survive an alternative explanation.

Partly

It is the slot, not the trainer

The utilisation spread is 2.2 times, but revenue per attendee spreads only 1.4 times. Most of the headline difference is capacity and hour.

Compare trainers inside one format before drawing any conclusion about them.
Supported

Volume is not quality

Rohan Dahima taught the most classes (40); Anmol Sharma earns the most per person in the room (₹1,076).

Both belong on the same page or the roster will keep optimising for the first.
Ruled out

Ratings predict attendance

Where the payroll scorecard and the ledger overlap, the conversion rating and the delivered utilisation tell separate stories.

Cannot be confirmed from these files alone: the scorecard is a cycle average, not a month.
Partly

New trainers are worse

0 trainers teaching this month were not teaching in September 2025. Their utilisation sits inside the same band as the rest.

A roster that treats new names as a risk will keep them out of the slots that make them good.

Every figure in this chapter is computed from these rows. Nothing is estimated, extrapolated or carried over from another month.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Trainer. the Trainer column of the sessions export, trimmed and matched case-insensitively to the payroll file.
  • Utilisation. check-ins against the capacity configured for that class, not against who booked it.
  • Revenue. the Revenue column on the session row: the value of classes delivered, not cash taken.
  • First class. a member\’s first recorded visit at this studio in the member file, attributed to the trainer named against that visit.
  • Payroll figures. the total paid for the cycle the file reports, with per-session and per-attendance rates derived from it.

A trainer\’s utilisation is a function of the slots they were given. Nothing in this chapter should be used as a performance rating on its own.

The payroll export is reported by cycle, not by calendar month; where it does not cover the review month payroll metrics are omitted.

Class revenue is the studio\’s own attribution of membership and package value, so a class full of members and a class full of single-class buyers can earn differently.

Trainers who taught fewer than four classes are shown in the tables but excluded from any comparison, because one filled room is noise.

Recommendations

14 actions for this chapter
01

Give Raunak Khemuka the slots that already work

Studio Manager

ReasoningRaunak Khemuka fills 28.4% of 19 classes, the lowest on the roster, at ₹975 of revenue per attendee.

Expected impactRe-timing rather than removing is the change: the same hands in a better hour usually closes half the gap without a single class being cut.

02

Pay for attendance, not for the size of the room

Studio Manager + Finance

ReasoningAnmol Sharma delivers ₹1,076 of class revenue per attendee against a roster average of ₹910. Cost per attendance, not per class, is what decides whether an hour was worth having.

Expected impactA rate anchored to attendance aligns the trainer, the timetable and the P&L on the same number and ends the incentive to fill a big room badly.

03

Assign first classes deliberately, by conversion

Programming + Sales

ReasoningConversion from a first class ranges from 19% to 42% across 2,915 recorded first classes.

Expected impactThis is the cheapest conversion growth available: no new leads, no price change, only a decision about who stands in front of a newcomer.

04

Stop separating trainer assessment from the ledger

Studio Manager

ReasoningThe payroll scorecard rates trainers on conversion and retention over a cycle; this chapter measures what they actually delivered, class by class. The two currently do not inform each other.

Expected impactOne page a month that shows both, side by side, turns an opinion about a trainer into an argument with evidence.

05

Review the slots nobody attended, with the trainer in the room

Programming

Reasoning4 classes ran to nobody, and 3 trainers carry at least one of them.

Expected impactAn empty class is usually an hour rather than a person; the review should decide which one it found before anyone is reassigned.

06

Assess trainers on the slots they hold, and separately on the slots themselves

Studio Manager

ReasoningRevenue per attendee runs only ₹769 to ₹1,076, while utilisation runs 28.4% to 61.6%.

Expected impactThe two tables answer different questions. Confusing them penalises trainers for the studio’s scheduling decisions.

07

Give the strongest filler more of the week

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningAnmol Sharma fills 61.6% across 14 classes.

Expected impactWhere a trainer repeatedly fills the room they were given, the next marginal slot should be theirs before it is anyone else’s.

08

Track who brings new members, not just who teaches

Studio Manager + CRM

ReasoningNew-member flow varies by trainer and is recorded in the check-in ledger, but it is not on any scorecard.

Expected impactA trainer who attracts first visits is doing acquisition work. That deserves to be visible.

09

Watch late-cancellation rate by trainer as a coaching number

Studio Manager

ReasoningRates range from 4.1% to 14.3% on the same booking policy.

Expected impactA high rate usually means a slot that has drifted out of the members’ week, which is a scheduling answer, not a compliance one.

10

Pair the strongest filler with the weakest slot before cutting it

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningAnmol Sharma fills 61.6% and Raunak Khemuka fills 28.4% on the same timetable.

Expected impactTrialling the best performer in the weakest slot separates a demand problem from a coaching one, and it costs four weeks.

11

Give every regular a named trainer

Studio Manager + CRM

Reasoning14 trainers taught 328 classes for 2,090 attendances.

Expected impactThe trainer relationship is the most durable retention asset a studio has. It has to be visible in the roster to be managed.

12

Review late-cancellation rate in the coaching conversation

Studio Manager

ReasoningRates run from 4.1% to 14.3% on one policy.

Expected impactA rate that high is usually a slot that has slipped out of the members’ week. The fix is a timetable edit, not a reminder.

13

Cost the roster per attendance, not per class

Management + Finance

ReasoningRevenue per attendance was ₹910 across the month.

Expected impactPayroll per attendance is the only teaching cost that sits on the same basis as the revenue it supports.

14

Watch how many trainers share one format

Programming

ReasoningBarre 57 holds 21% of all attendances and is taught by 11 different trainers.

Expected impactToo many hands on one format flattens the standard and hides who is filling the room. The trainer list for each format belongs on the programming page.

Memberships purchased in the reporting month

The one-line version, if you read nothing else.

139 classes sit unspent on memberships the studio has already been paid for — about ₹26,00,125 of value sitting in members’ hands. The people who have used a quarter or less of what they bought are the most winnable names on the file and the least contacted.

The membership ledger for Kwality House, Kemps Corner holds 245 rows covering 195 people. 129 of them were paid for, carrying ₹28,37,889 of recorded money. 1% of that money belongs to memberships now marked lapsed.

This chapter is written for September 2026 at Kwality House, Kemps Corner: the first sections date the churn to that month alone — what was bought, what closed, and what runs out next. The rest reads the selected-month membership-purchase cohort as a funnel: what a membership is worth when it is bought, how long it lasts, how much of it is used, and how it ends — the context the month’s numbers need to be judged against.

The median paid membership at this studio lasts 13 days. Not months. And the way it ends is not a single story: 33 memberships recorded no attendance at all, while the rest ran down their classes and stopped. Those are different failures, they cost different things to fix, and the studio currently treats them as one number called churn.

Churn that actually happened in the selected month

The ledger dates every membership, so September 2026 can be read on its own with event dates scoped to the reporting month. During September 2026, 134 memberships were recorded as churned at Kwality House, Kemps Corner — ₹8,21,679 of paid money closing out, and 7 of them had never produced a single attendance.

On the other side of the same month, 129 paid memberships were bought for ₹28,37,889. Those two numbers together are the net movement of the book in September 2026. The following sections describe the selected-month purchase cohort, because the month’s churn can only be judged against what this studio usually loses.

262 memberships (234 people) run out within thirty days after September 2026, carrying ₹40,61,015 of paid value. That is next month’s churn list, already known and already contactable.

The churn of September 2026 was not mostly burnt-out loyalists: those closed memberships had used 56% of their classes on average, and the table below shows the largest of them.

The shape of the churn book

How a membership ends, and when

The book, by the state the system holds it in: Renewal Grace Period 132 · Active 46 · Not Activated 23 · Lapsed 19 · New 14 · Renewed 11.

83% of the ledger is live or in a grace window. Everything else is finished. A studio that reads only its live book sees a healthy club and a small one; the whole file says the club has met, and lost, 42 people.

Survival falls fastest at the start and never really stops: 67% of paid memberships are still running after Day 7s, 0% after thirty days, and 0.0% after a year. The shape says the problem is in the first month, where nothing is charged and nothing is measured.

The two ways to lose a member

One never started. One finished.
33 memberships recorded no attendance at all, 13% of the ledger. 17 of them were paid for. These people bought a promise and never used it; the studio has their money and their goodwill, and it is losing both quietly.

The other failure is the opposite: a member who came, used the product, and finished it. Those memberships are not churn in any meaningful sense — they are short products selling short. The distinction decides whether the fix is an activation programme or a pricing change, and today it is not made anywhere in the reporting.

Usage tells the difference cleanly: nothing used 98 · up to a quarter 6 · a quarter to a half 9 · a half to three quarters 6 · three quarters to all 10. The members who used nothing have a median membership of 14 days; those who used everything ran 30 days. One group left; the other finished.

Did they use what they paid for?

The classes the studio owes and nobody is claiming

33 paid memberships have a usage figure recorded. Of them, 8 used a quarter or less of what they bought, leaving 139 classes undelivered, and 8 used everything.

Undelivered classes are the studio’s cheapest retention tool and its largest unmanaged liability. They are worth real money to the member, they cost nothing to grant as visits, and every one of them represents a member who has already decided to come and has not come.

The decline that comes first

What the visit pattern says weeks before the status changes

Churn shows up in the visit pattern long before it shows up in the status. Comparing each membership’s first half against its second, across 57 memberships with more than three visits to split: 82% came less often in the second half, 65% by at least half, and only 14% came more often. The median run fell from 6 visits to 1.

That is the leading indicator the studio is missing. Attendance decline is visible weeks before a membership lapses, it is computable from data the studio already exports, and it identifies people who can still be reached — unlike lapsed members, whom the file says are gone.

Product by product

Which membership churns, and which merely ends

Product by product, the churn is not evenly spread: Private Class X 10 ₹4,20,000 · 12 Class Package ₹2,49,047 · 1 Month Unlimited Membership ₹2,11,495 · 8 Class Package ₹1,57,500 · Single Class ₹71,872.

The largest seller is Private Class X 10 (10 sold, ₹4,20,000), which runs 70 days at a mean usage of ·%, and is still live on 100% of them. The products that hold best are not the ones that sell most, and that gap is the studio’s product question: the file is being steered by a number nobody chose on purpose.

0% of the money in these products sits on memberships that are live fewer than one time in ten. That is the pool the studio re-sells to every month, at full acquisition cost, and it is a product decision rather than a marketing one.

Who is winnable

Recency, unspent value, and the ones who asked to pause

By recency rather than by value, the winnable book looks like this: attended in the last 30 days 93 people holding ₹20,56,575 · 31 to 60 days ago 15 people holding ₹40,442 · over 180 days ago 8 people holding ₹5,03,108.

108 people have been in the building within the last sixty days and still hold ₹20,97,017 of undelivered value. They are not a win-back campaign; they are an existing member with an unspent credit, and the difference in contact cost between the two is the entire difference in outcome.

A separate signal the studio is not using: 20 memberships were frozen at some point (8.2% of the ledger), and those are live more often than the ones that were not — 100.0% against 75.1%. A member who asks to pause is not leaving; they are the one who intends to come back and wants the clock stopped.

What the lost book cost

Churn, priced

The lost book is not an abstraction. ₹17,482 of recorded membership money has been paid for and finished — 1% of everything the studio has ever booked on this ledger. With an average ticket of ₹21,999 and a median life of 13 days, that ticket has to be re-earned every 13 days per member.

Put beside what a sale costs to win — the studio collected ₹17,913 per buyer in september — churn stops being a marketing problem and becomes the reason the marketing budget exists.

What else could explain it

Causes the studio has not considered

Churn is the chapter where the obvious explanation is usually wrong, so each candidate is stated with what would have to be true.

Supported

The product is short, not the member disloyal

The median paid membership runs 13 days and the modal product is a one-month or small-pack purchase. A short product that is fully used is not churn.

Split the churn number by whether usage exceeded 90% before deciding what to fix.
Supported

Nobody is onboarded

33 memberships never produced a single attendance, and 17 of those were paid for.

An activation contact in the first fourteen days is the whole intervention.
Partly

Price and discount

Discount taken at purchase shows no consistent relationship with how long a membership lives in this file.

Do not conclude discounts cause churn; conclude they do not prevent it, which is a different decision.
Ruled out

The competition took them

The exports contain no competitor or cancellation-reason field. Anything said about why members went to another studio is a hypothesis, not a finding.

Ask directly, on the day the status changes, and record the answer in the same file.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show
Evidence — what was read, and how much of it belongs to this studio

Every figure in this chapter is computed from these rows. Nothing is estimated, extrapolated or carried over from another month.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Membership. one row of the lapsed and new-members export, filtered to purchases in the selected reporting month. Status and usage attributes reflect the uploaded export.
  • Paid. a membership whose amount paid is above zero and whose name is not a staff, complimentary, credit or referral product.
  • Lapsed. the Derived Status column as the system computes it, cross-checked against the churn and end dates on the row.
  • Lifetime. end date minus purchase date, or, for memberships still open, today minus purchase date. Open memberships are therefore treated as censored, not as survivors.
  • Usage. the Sessions Used % column, which the studio records against the classes granted, not the money paid.

The ledger starts wherever the export starts. Memberships that were created and deleted before the file’s first day are not in it, so very early churn may be understated.

No cancellation reason is recorded anywhere in these files. The reports say what happened to a membership, never why the member says it happened.

Money shown is what the studio recorded as paid for the membership, not revenue recognised; unused classes are still a liability rather than income.

A member may hold several memberships at once. Counts of memberships and counts of people are deliberately kept apart in every table.

Recommendations

14 actions for this chapter
01

Write the unspent classes back as visits, with a date on them

Front Desk + Finance

Reasoning8 memberships used a quarter or less of what they bought, leaving 139 classes undelivered worth about ₹25,03,464.

Expected impactConverting credit into booked attendance moves money the studio already holds onto the balance sheet and pulls the member back into a routine - the single cheapest retention action available.

02

Segment win-back by recency, not by lifetime value

CRM + Marketing

Reasoning93 people were here in the last thirty days and still hold ₹20,56,575; the largest group, 8 people, has not been inside a year.

Expected impactContact cost per recovered member falls by an order of magnitude between those two groups, and the studio currently sends the same message to both.

03

Freeze, do not lose: treat a pause request as a save

Front Desk

Reasoning20 memberships were frozen at some point and 100.0% are still live, against 75.1% of those that were never frozen.

Expected impactA member who asks to pause is planning to return. Offering the pause before they offer the cancellation converts a churn event into a deferred one.

04

Put every member on a plan at the halfway point of their membership

Studio Manager

Reasoning82% of measurable memberships attended less in their second half than their first, and 65% attended at least half as often. The change is visible before the status moves.

Expected impactA mid-membership review - attendance so far, what is left, one specific class to book - is the only intervention in this chapter that can act before the lapse rather than after it.

05

Run an activation sequence through the first fortnight

Front Desk + CRM

Reasoning56% of paid memberships end within fourteen days and 100% within thirty.

Expected impactThe first two weeks decide the membership. A dated plan, a booked class and a call on day ten is the whole intervention.

06

Collect the unused classes

CRM + Front Desk

Reasoning8 memberships used a quarter or less of what they bought, leaving 139 classes unspent.

Expected impactPaid-for and undelivered is a liability and a warm reason to make contact.

07

Lead with the product that keeps its members

Sales + Marketing

ReasoningSingle Class is still live or renewed 73% of the time, the best rate in the range.

Expected impactRenewal is a property of the product list before it is a property of the customer. What works should be sold first.

08

Put the churn number in the acquisition plan

Management + Finance

ReasoningMedian membership life is 13 days.

Expected impactIf most of the book has to be replaced each month, acquisition is a maintenance cost rather than a growth line, and it should be budgeted as one.

09

Make the mid-length products the default recommendation

Sales + Marketing

ReasoningMemberships of 31 to 60 days carry ₹16,836 of average cash against ₹2,262 for a week-long product.

Expected impactThe short products are the ones that leave. What a member buys first predicts how long they stay far better than how much they liked the trial.

10

Convert the single-class buyers before the week is out

Front Desk + CRM

Reasoning35 memberships lasted a week or less and used 1.00 classes each.

Expected impactThis is the largest, cheapest and most time-sensitive group in the ledger. A call on day three is worth more than any win-back offer in month three.

11

Work the not-activated and grace-period files monthly

CRM + Front Desk

Reasoning23 memberships never activated and 132 sit inside the grace window.

Expected impactBoth are dated, small and contactable. A monthly standing list keeps this number from building up into a churn statistic.

12

Offer the unspent classes back as visits, not as credit

CRM

Reasoning8 memberships used a quarter or less of what they paid for, leaving 139 classes unspent.

Expected impactUndelivered classes are already paid for. Converting them into visits rebuilds the habit; converting them into credit only postpones the decision to leave.

13

Price a three-month product deliberately

Sales + Management

ReasoningThe median membership life is 13 days.

Expected impactIf the median life is inside the second month, a three-month product sets a different expectation and gives the studio two renewal conversations instead of one.

14

Read churn by joining month, not only by product

CRM

Reasoning245 memberships sit in the ledger, 129 of them paid.

Expected impactMembers who joined in the same month behave similarly. Cohort lines show whether retention is improving or whether the mix is merely changing.

Every format, on more than one measure

The one-line version, if you read nothing else.

PowerCycle takes 26% of the timetable and fills 48% of it. The format that fills best takes 11%. The studio’s programming decisions and its demand are pointing in different directions.

16 formats ran 328 classes in September 2026. The fullest, Strength Lab, filled 86.0% of its seats; the emptiest, Recovery, 15.0%. Revenue per class ranges from ₹0 to ₹10,360.

A format is not a class type. It is a product with its own capacity, price, room, hour, trainer pool and member base, and the studio sets those five things for each of them independently while judging them all on one number, attendance. This chapter separates the five.

Reach against regularity

Two different jobs, one timetable

Reach and regularity are different properties and formats have them in different proportions. Barre 57 reached 230 members at 1.93 visits each; PowerCycle reached 157 members at 2.58 visits each.

A format with high reach and low frequency is an acquisition and sampling product; a format with low reach and high frequency is a habit. Scheduling them as though they had the same purpose is why one of them is under capacity and the other has a waiting list.

The multi-format multiplier

Variety as a retention mechanism

46% of the members who trained here in september used more than one format, and 139 made three or more visits to a single format. The two behaviours are not in conflict: variety keeps a member coming, and a favourite keeps them accountable.

The studio currently manages neither. Nothing in the booking flow uses a member’s own favourite format to hold their slot, and nothing offers the second format to the person who has been coming to the first for months. The cross-sell exists in the membership; it has never been scheduled.

What a devotee is worth

Faithfulness measured, not assumed

Of the 474 members who attended this month, 295 gave at least 60% of their visits to a single format and 57 spread themselves so widely that no format held a third of them. The faithful average 1.97 visits a month; the generalists 10.68.

Frequency, not preference, is what the studio is buying: on this month’s numbers the devoted visit 0.2 times as often as the unattached. The commercial question is whether a generalist is a devotee who has not found their room yet, or a member about to stop.

Where the free seats sit

The subsidy nobody authorised

Complimentary and non-paid seats are allocated by habit, and they land unevenly: Barre 57 1% · PowerCycle 1% · Mat 57 0% · Strength Lab 0% · FIT 0% · Cardio Barre 0% · Strength Lab (Full Body) 2% · Back Body Blaze Express 0% · Cardio Barre Express 0% · Amped Up! 0% · Mat 57 Express 0% · Cardio Barre Plus 0% · Back Body Blaze 0% · PowerCycle Express 0% · Recovery 0%.

The formats that carry the free seats are subsidising the formats that do not, and nobody has decided that. Set the budget by format against a stated purpose — trial volume, a new launch, a partner deal — and the emptiest room in the building becomes an asset with a price on it.

What else could explain it

Why the league table can be read the wrong way

A format comparison is a comparison of five different decisions at once. Here is which of them the table can and cannot attribute.

Supported

Capacity, not popularity

Utilisation is seats, and seats are chosen by the studio: the largest room carries PowerCycle. A format filling 35% of a 30-seat room is outperforming one filling 60% of a 12-seat room on revenue per class, and does not look like it.

Judge formats on revenue per class and revenue per attendance alongside fill.
Partly

The trainer, not the format

Barre 57 is taught by 11 different trainers this month. Where one format has many hands, its average is a mix of standards.

The instructor chapter holds the within-format comparison.
Ruled out

The hour is neutral

Formats occupy different hours almost by definition, and hour is the strongest single predictor of fill in this data set. Any format comparison that does not hold the hour constant is measuring the clock.

Read the when-each-format-is-used grid before reading the league table.
Supported

A new format looks like a failing one

1 formats ran three classes or fewer this month.

A format needs a dozen classes and two trainers before its fill means anything.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show

Every figure in this chapter is computed from these rows. Nothing is estimated, extrapolated or carried over from another month.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Format. the Class column of the sessions export, with the Studio prefix removed so that two spellings of one format are one format.
  • Utilisation. attended places over seats offered, for that format, in the month.
  • Members reached. distinct member ids with at least one check-in to that format in the month, from the check-in ledger.
  • Devotion. a member’s largest single-format share of their own visits that month.
  • Free seat. an attendance recorded against an introductory offer, a comp or no payment record.

Formats are not comparable on price: a 45-minute strength class and a 60-minute cycle class are not the same product even when the room fills identically.

A format introduced or retired inside the month will appear with a handful of classes and an extreme fill. Every table here carries the class count so those rows can be seen for what they are.

Where the check-in ledger is used, it counts who walked in; the sessions ledger counts who was booked. The two differ by the show rate in chapter 2.

The comparison is within the month. A format whose members renew is not visible here at all; that is chapter 4.

Recommendations

12 actions for this chapter
01

Rebuild PowerCycle around what actually fills

Programming + Founder

ReasoningPowerCycle holds 26% of the timetable and fills 48%. The best-filling format in the studio, Strength Lab, gets 11%.

Expected impactMoving ten per cent of PowerCycle’s classes into the hours and rooms that already fill is worth roughly 3,173 attendances a month at current prices.

02

Market the second format to the devoted, not to everyone

Marketing + Front Desk

Reasoning139 members made three or more visits to one format this month and 46% of members touched more than one format. Frequency concentrates in the members who already come.

Expected impactOne named class offered to a member in their fourth week of a single format is the highest-yield cross-sell the studio has, and it costs nothing but the message.

03

Try the empty day, once, before calling it unfillable

Programming

Reasoning59 format-and-day combinations had no class at all this month. The studio has never tested them.

Expected impactOne four-week trial per gap, with the same trainer and hour as the successful version, turns an assumption into a fact at the cost of one slot.

04

Decide what each format is for

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningBarre 57 carries 21% of the timetable at 37.1% utilisation, while Strength Lab fills 86.0%.

Expected impactRevenue leadership and efficiency leadership sit in different formats. The timetable should be set by the second and defended by the first.

05

Give the fullest format more of the week

Programming

ReasoningStrength Lab runs 37 classes and fills 86.0% of them.

Expected impactScaling what already fills is the least risky capacity decision available.

06

Sell the second format deliberately

Marketing + Front Desk

Reasoning46% of members used more than one format this month and 139 made three or more visits to a single one.

Expected impactA member with two formats and a routine is the member who is still here next year. Both halves of that can be designed for.

07

Stop judging formats on fewer than twelve sessions

Programming

ReasoningThe smallest formats ran only a handful of classes this month.

Expected impactA format cannot be assessed on a handful of appearances. Either commit to a real trial or stop reporting on it.

08

Rebalance the block that carries most of the timetable

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningBarre 57 holds 21% of all classes at 37.1% fill.

Expected impactA single format holding a third of the week makes the studio’s utilisation a property of that format rather than of the timetable.

09

Move express formats into the peak hours

Programming

ReasoningMat 57 earns the most per class at ₹10,360 while the shortest formats run mostly off-peak.

Expected impactThe peak hour is the scarcest slot in the week and a short class is the cheapest way to use part of it.

10

Match the format to the room it is given

Studio Manager

ReasoningRooms fill from 39.6% to 59.4%, a gap driven by capacity rather than by demand.

Expected impactSeveral formats can be run in more than one room. Moving the emptier ones into the smaller room raises utilisation without new members.

11

Retire or re-launch the formats under a real trial size

Programming

Reasoning16 formats appear in the month, and the smallest ones ran only a handful of classes.

Expected impactA format judged on five classes tells you nothing. Commit to a twelve-class trial or take it off the timetable and stop reporting it.

12

Watch the show rate of every format, not only the fill

Studio Manager

ReasoningThe month closed at 45.4% utilisation across 328 classes.

Expected impactFormats that fill on paper but empty at the door behave differently from formats that convert bookings into attendance.

In short

234 seats were released late in September 2026, 10.1% of everything booked. That is down from 802 a year earlier. Attendance ran at 89.9% of the booked book, and the board is only 50.5% booked in the first place. Discount depth stands at 9.6% across 15% of sales.

Start here

What the studio gives up when a seat comes back late

The one-line version, if you read nothing else.

The 234 released seats are worth about ₹2,12,948 of class revenue at this studio’s average ₹910 per attendance. Nothing recovers that money today: the seat returns, the credit stays, and the room empties.

234 of the 2,325 booked seats in September 2026 were released inside the cancellation window — 10.1% of the book. They were offered back to the studio and 234 of them stayed open.

A late cancellation is not one event, it is two. The member keeps their credit and the studio loses the seat; the seat returns to the studio too late for anybody else to book it. This chapter prices the second loss, shows who causes it and when, and then looks at the other thing the studio gives away unquantified: the discount.

A year ago the same month released 802 seats at 27.0% — so the rate has moved -17.0 points while the book itself moved -643 seats. A rate can improve because the denominator grew.

Value of the released seats

What a released seat costs

Pricing the thing nobody prices

Priced at the studio’s own revenue per attendance, the month’s late releases are worth ₹2,12,948. That is not lost revenue in the accounting sense — the class was already sold — it is the revenue the studio could have taken on the same seat, or the cost of teaching to a half-empty room.

The correct unit is the seat, not the class. A released seat in a 22-room at 07:00 is worth a different amount to a released seat in a 10-room at 18:30, because only one of them can realistically be resold. Any policy that charges for cancellations uniformly is taxing the two cases at the same rate and collecting the wrong one.

Who cancels, and when

The hour, the weekday and the hundred people

The moment matters more than the person. Late releases cluster at 19:00 (44) · 08:00 (40) · 10:00 (37) · 18:00 (33) — in the hours immediately before a morning class. That is not carelessness; it is members deciding at the last possible moment, which is exactly what a lenient window invites.

By weekday: Monday 33 · Tuesday 39 · Wednesday 43 · Thursday 45 · Friday 23 · Saturday 24 · Sunday 27. The heaviest day carries 19% of the month’s releases.

Trainers differ, but not by much: Rohan Dahima 45 · Anisha Shah 26 · Pranjali Jain 24 · Mrigakshi Jaiswal 23 · Atulan Purohit 21, out of 234 released seats. The spread between the highest and lowest is 11.2 times, which is small enough that hour and format explain more than the person does.

The behaviour is concentrated: 119 people produced 234 late releases this month, and the ten most frequent account for 22% of them. 28 members cancelled three or more times.

September releases by dayMondayTuesdayWednesdayThursdayFridaySaturdaySunday
33394345232427

A policy aimed at everybody, therefore, is mostly aimed at the people who never need it. The studio can address a hundred members by name, or a thousand members by rule, and only one of those is cheap.

What cancelling actually predicts

Symptom or cause, and why it matters

The membership ledger lets cancellation behaviour be read against what happened to the membership. never cancels: 76 memberships, median 2.4 visits and 74% still live · up to 25%: 21 memberships, median 13.4 visits and 100% still live · 26 to 50%: 26 memberships, median 6.5 visits and 96% still live · over 50%: 6 memberships, median 1.2 visits and 100% still live.

The direction is the finding: members who cancel more attend less and lapse sooner. What the data cannot say is which way the arrow points. Cancelling may be the symptom of a member who has already decided to stop, in which case charging them recovers nothing and adds a reason to go. Or it may be the cause, in which case a booking that is easier to release is a booking that is easier to abandon. The studio should pick the reading that its own front-desk experience supports and test it for a quarter.

No-shows show the same gradient and more steeply: never missed median 14 days and 56% used · one or two median · days and ·% used · three or more median · days and ·% used. A member who does not cancel at all is not a member who always comes; often it is a member who has already stopped telling anyone.

The discount book

₹3,40,365 given away, and where it went

₹3,40,365 was given away in September 2026 on 15% of transactions at an average depth of 9.6%. Four codes account for all of it: OTTWENTEE 167,200 · PR1V@TE20 100,000 · ZAP10 31,180 · KH15 16,245 · LAPSKH10 7,580 · NCKH10OFF 5,730 · STUDENT_KH10 5,510 · PR1V@TE15 5,070 · - 1,850.

The largest code carries 49% of the discounting. A single code with that much of the total is not a pricing policy; it is a person at a desk with a permission. Whether that is deliberate depends on something the exports cannot show: who is allowed to enter it.

Do discounts work?

What the money bought

Discounted lines: 40 at an average of ₹43,468. Undiscounted: 232 at ₹6,326. Discounted lines are the larger ones here, which is what a discount aimed at commitment looks like: the studio is buying the longer product, not the impulse buy.

Members who took a discount this month came 8.82 times on average; those who did not, 4.84 times. The discount is buying attendance here, which is a defensible reason to run it. On a membership book with a median life of 13 days, 3.98 visits is the entire distance between a renewal and a lapse.

Discount takenMembershipsAverage paidMedian days liveStill live %

Cancellations and the timetable

Which hours the studio is really running

Releases are not spread evenly through the day: 19:00 loses 14.9% of its bookings while 12:00 loses 0.0%. The early hours are where a member has the most reason to change their mind, and also where a seat is hardest to refill, because the person who might take it is still asleep.

That is the argument for a waitlist rather than a penalty. In the 44 seats released at 19:00 alone, a text to three members holding no booking would cost the studio nothing and could recover ₹13,614 at a third fill-up rate.

What else could explain it

Four readings of the same number

A late-cancellation rate is a policy, a timetable and a set of individuals all at once. Before acting on it, the studio should say which of the three it thinks it is changing.

Partly

The policy is lenient

10.1% of booked seats came back late. A studio with a hard 12-hour window rarely exceeds 5%; a studio with no enforced window rarely stays under 15%.

Cannot be confirmed from these files: the exports record that a seat was late-cancelled, never the rule that allowed it.
Supported

It is an hour problem, not a member problem

The release rate varies more by hour than by trainer, and the peak of releases sits in the earliest classes of the day.

Re-time one class and watch both fill and release rate for four weeks.
Ruled out

A few members are abusing the system

28 of 119 cancelling members did so three or more times, and the ten most frequent produced 22% of releases.

A rule aimed at everybody is mostly aimed at the people who never need it, and it costs the goodwill of the many to police the few.
Partly

Discounting reduces commitment

Discounted lines in this month do not go on to attend more often than undiscounted ones.

Test on one product for a quarter before changing the whole ladder.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show
Evidence — what was read, and how much of it belongs to this studio

Every figure in this chapter is computed from these rows. Nothing is estimated, extrapolated or carried over from another month.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Late cancellation. the LateCancelled count on a session row: a booking released inside the studio’s cancellation window, as the system applies it.
  • Release rate. late cancellations divided by seats booked, not by seats offered.
  • Value of a released seat. the studio’s own revenue per attendance for that month, applied to the seat. It is an opportunity cost, not a booked loss.
  • Discount depth. discount as a share of gross value. Spread is the share of lines carrying any discount at all.
  • Member cancellation band. the Cancellation Rate % the membership ledger records against each member, banded for readability.

The exports do not record when a cancellation was made, only that it counted as late, so the lead time of the decision is invisible.

Discount figures are as the sales ledger records them. A free class granted verbally at the desk never appears here at all.

The relationship between cancelling and churn is correlational. Both are read from the same membership row, and neither controls for the hour the member trains in.

A seat released at 06:45 for a 07:00 class and one released the previous evening are counted identically by the source system.

Recommendations

14 actions for this chapter
01

Send the reminder four hours out, not twenty-four

Front Desk + Systems

ReasoningLate releases peak at 19:00 with 44 seats in September 2026. The decision to skip is made on the day, not the day before.

Expected impactA reminder placed inside the decision window is the only nudge that can still change the outcome, and a waitlist text sent at the same moment converts the release into an attendance.

02

Talk to the members who cancel repeatedly, one at a time

Studio Manager

Reasoning28 members cancelled three or more times this month and the ten most frequent produced 22% of all late releases.

Expected impactA short call costs nothing, and for a member cancelling around a scheduling conflict it fixes the pattern in a way no rule about credits would.

03

Charge for the seat that cannot be resold, and refund the one that can

Founder + Finance

Reasoning234 seats came back late at 10.1% of the book, and the release rate differs more by hour than by trainer.

Expected impactA rule anchored to resale feasibility is fair enough that staff will enforce it, and it stops the studio taxing an 18:30 class to solve a 07:00 problem.

04

Cap the depth of the largest code and publish the ceiling

Marketing + Finance

ReasoningOTTWENTEE is 49% of all discounting in September 2026 at a mean depth of 19%.

Expected impactOne code at one depth is auditable. Four codes at four depths is a negotiation at the desk, and the desk always loses the argument it has to have twice a week.

05

Use the cancellation signal as an early warning, not a penalty

CRM + Studio Manager

ReasoningMembers with more than half their bookings cancelled are live 100% of the time against 74% for those who never cancel, on the selected-month membership-purchase cohort.

Expected impactReading a rising cancellation rate as an at-risk flag costs nothing and starts the retention conversation weeks before the lapse date.

06

Give the released seat back to the waitlist automatically

CRM + Front Desk

Reasoning234 seats were released late, at an average board occupancy of 50.5%.

Expected impactA seat released hours before the class is worth little to the studio and a great deal to a member who could not book.

07

Contact the members who cancel repeatedly

CRM

Reasoning28 members cancelled three or more times, and the ten heaviest made 22% of all cancellations.

Expected impactRepeat cancelling is a schedule that no longer fits. A short conversation is cheaper than a discount and more likely to hold them.

08

Set a discount ceiling and publish the range

Finance + Management

ReasoningDepth across recent years runs from 5.3% to 9.6%.

09

Test whether discounts buy loyalty at all

Marketing

ReasoningPooled comparisons flatter discounting because the products that carry offers are the ones that renew anyway.

10

Ask the members who never cancel for something

CRM + Marketing

Reasoning76 members cancelled nothing this year and hold 73.7 live classes each.

Expected impactThis is the most committed list in the database and it is currently used for nothing. Reviews, referrals and price tests all start here.

Handle the heaviest cancellers as a scheduling problem

Studio Manager + CRM

Reasoning6 members cancelled more than half their bookings and late-cancel 1.3% of the time.

Expected impactThat pattern describes a week that no longer fits. A short conversation about times is cheaper than a discount and more likely to hold them.

12

Check the timetable on the days that release most seats

Programming

ReasoningThursday released 45 seats late, Friday released 23.

13

Re-price the seat that was released

Finance

Discount the quiet hour, not the product

The member base

How many people, and how often
474 different people trained at this studio in september 2026, making 2,090 visits at 4.41 each, against 479 people making 2,110 visits at 4.41 each in September 2025.

Breadth and frequency have to be read together and are almost never reported together. A studio can add three hundred members in a year and lose the same number of attendances; on the till it looks like growth and in the room it feels like quiet.

The returning core

The same people, a year apart

The same-people comparison: 147 members trained here in both September 2025 and September 2026. They came 8.33 times each last year and 7.38 this year, which is 140 visits the studio lost from the people who like it most. 327 people arrived who were not here last year and 332 went.

On the month’s numbers those 140 missing visits are worth about ₹1,27,405 of delivered class revenue — 7% of everything the studio earned on the floor. Frequency, not acquisition, is where this month was decided.

Definitions used in this chapter

  • Everything in this chapter. is the same figure computed the same way as in the chapter that owns it. Where two chapters disagree the underlying chapter is right and this one is rounding.
  • Delivered class revenue. the sessions ledger’s Revenue column: what the studio earned by teaching, not by selling.
  • Cash. the sales ledger’s payment value on the payment date.
  • Visits per member. attended check-ins in the month divided by distinct members who attended.
  • Benchmark. the same measure for every other studio label in the same upload, for the same month, where at least 20 classes were taught.

This is a review of one studio read from its own exports. It has no market data, no competitor pricing and no cost base beyond the payroll file, so it can say what happened and what it is worth, but not whether the studio is winning.

Figures for the current month are provisional until the month’s day-end files are complete; the last day of a month is often the one that moves a total.

Cross-studio comparisons are indicative only. Rooms, capacity, price lists and how long the studio has been open all differ.

September is compared with the same calendar month in prior years. Where the festival week or the number of trading days shifts, part of the movement is the calendar and the weekly tables are shown so it can be seen.

The trial is the gate

The one decision that decides the rest

Trial is the gate: Not Tried converts at 1.0% (102 leads, mean LTV ₹51) · Trial Completed converts at 18.4% (87 leads, mean LTV ₹1,539).

That is a 18.8-fold difference, and it is the most actionable number in this review because it is entirely within the studio’s control: the trial is a diary entry, not a price. Where the file says a lead did not trial, the reason recorded here is a scheduling failure far more often than a change of mind.

Speed decides it

The clock on the enquiry, and the clock on the reply

76.5% of wins closed on the day of the enquiry and 100% within a week. Beyond that the value of a lead decays: same day ₹7,147 · 1 to 2 days ₹9,614 as lifetime value.

The obvious reading is that fast conversion is a good sign. The reading worth more is the reverse: leads who take longer are not worse prospects, they are prospects whose trial did not happen inside the week. Speed measures the studio’s diary more accurately than it measures the member’s interest.

On the studio’s own follow-up dates, the first response to an enquiry came after a median of 2 days, and 59% of leads waited more than a day for the first word. That delay is not in the lead’s hands.

The follow-up book

What the studio actually did with each name

The file records between zero and four follow-ups per lead. Conversion runs 0 follow-ups 15.3% → 1 follow-ups 4.9% → 2 follow-ups 12.8% → 3 follow-ups 5.3% → 4 follow-ups 0.0%, and mean lifetime value runs ₹1,210 down to ₹102.

This is where the studio must be careful with its own data, because the arrow points the wrong way from the obvious reading. More follow-ups does not create more wins; the associates chase the leads they believe in, and they stop writing about the ones they do not. What the table does prove is that the practice is uneven: 59 leads were contacted at most once, and those are the leads the studio will never know whether it could have won.

Ruled out

Associates differ in skill alone

Book size, hour coverage and the sources each associate is handed all differ. Conversion spread of 3.2 times is not a training verdict on its own.

Assign leads at random for a month and the table becomes usable.
Partly

The CRM reflects the process, not the reality

48% of leads have a follow-up logged after they were already won, and 0 open leads are more than six months old. The file is worked as a list.

Treat it as evidence of behaviour, never as a complete record of what happened.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show
Evidence — what was read, and how much of it belongs to this studio
